conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you until your kidney function stabilizes, the antibiotics are underway, and your heart rhythm is safe. Probably a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your latest labs show your creatinine is down to 1.1 and potassium is 4.8 — much better. We’re stopping IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. How’s my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PR interval improved when we held diltiazem — from 330 to 202. We’ve restarted it at 180 mg daily. It’s now at 220, which is still prolonged but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The electrophysiology team reviewed your rhythm — you have some early extra beats, but they’re not dangerous. They think your AV block is from the diltiazem, not the carfilzomib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. My shoulder’s been hurting too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve continued your oxycodone and gabapentin for that. It’s likely from your myeloma or neuropathy. We’ll keep managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts? They’ve been low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 8.5 and platelets at 60 — still low, but not worsening. This is expected with your chemotherapy. We’re monitoring daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on lamivudine for hepatitis B — still need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it. Your liver tests are stable, and we don’t want the virus to reactivate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is showing improvement, and you’ve had no fever. We’re confident the pneumonia is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your kidney function is normal, heart rhythm is stable, and you’re feeling better overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still take the diltiazem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at 180 mg daily. We’ll follow up with cardiology to monitor the AV block. If it stays stable, no further action is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the levofloxacin — four more days. Then continue vancomycin for one more week after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my Ritalin? I’ve been on it for fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it for now. Stimulants can affect heart rhythm, and with your AV block, it’s safer to avoid it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. I’ll talk to my oncologist about other options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home. You’ll walk independently but may want your cane for longer distances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your oncology and cardiology appointments. Call if you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or irregular heartbeat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Get some rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been feeling weak, your heart has been racing, and you've had diarrhea at home. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doc. I’ve felt really tired for a few days. My heart was pounding, even when I was just sitting. And the diarrhea—started about three days ago, pretty bad. Also, my port site was sore when I touched it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for sharing. Given your history with multiple myeloma and your port, we’re concerned about infection. We’ve started some blood tests and will check your port site. We also need to rule out a recurrence of C. diff, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I remember that from last time. But I haven’t had diarrhea since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Sometimes symptoms improve once you’re hydrated and off certain meds. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with the weakness and fast heart rate, which could be from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My heart’s still fast though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rate is 110. You’re on carvedilol and diltiazem for rhythm control, but you haven’t taken them in a few days. We’ll restart them once we’re sure you’re stable and the infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried about my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia—your heart is just beating fast, not irregularly. No signs of a current heart attack, but we see some old changes. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood cultures. The first one came back negative, but we’re waiting on more. We’re starting IV vancomycin just in case, especially since you’re neutropenic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin again? I’ve been on that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because it covers a broad range of bacteria, especially with your port and history. We also tested your stool for C. diff—and it came back positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no, not again. So I need the oral vancomycin too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you oral vancomycin for 10 days to treat the C. diff, plus IV vancomycin for the bloodstream infection we’re concerned about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your second blood culture grew Strep gallolyticus—a gut bacteria that can get into the blood, especially with low immunity. It’s sensitive to vancomycin, so we’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s from my gut? Not the port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. These bacteria live in the intestines. With weakened immunity, they can translocate. We don’t think your port is infected, especially since the soreness is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I’ve been having more knee pain—both knees, but the right one is worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you have arthritis, but given your myeloma, we’re concerned the disease might be active in your bones. We’re ordering X-rays of both knees to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this mean the myeloma is getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. We saw plasma cells in your blood test, which is unusual. Your oncologist is concerned the disease is more aggressive. We’ll discuss treatment changes soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The knee X-rays are back. No fractures, but there’s a small lucent area in your right knee—could be a bone lesion. We’re not sure yet if it’s from myeloma or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should we get an MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oncologist reviewed it. Since we’re already changing your myeloma treatment, they want to monitor it closely as an outpatient. An MRI can wait unless the pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What’s changing with my treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were on pomalidomide and cyclophosphamide, but we’ve held them during the infection. Given the concern for progression, your team plans to switch to ixazomib after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. Is it pills or shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a pill, taken weekly. It’s similar to Velcade, which you’ve had before. You got one dose in the hospital to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I hope it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your repeat blood cultures are negative. That means the antibiotics are working. We’ll keep IV vancomycin for 10 days total from the last positive culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll still be on IV meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a few more days. A nurse will come to your home to give the IV vancomycin twice a day. Then you’ll finish the oral vancomycin for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s manageable. What about my blood counts? I remember they were low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white count and platelets were low—pancytopenia. Could be from infection, myeloma, or prior chemo. Your neutrophil count is improving with Neupogen. We gave you platelets and red cells yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a bit better after that. Any more transfusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll monitor. You’re eating better, which helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram to check for endocarditis—since you had bacteria in the blood. Good news: no sign of infection on your heart valves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild thickening of some valves and a slightly enlarged left atrium, but your heart function is normal. Nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My heart rate is slower now too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, down to 88. We restarted your carvedilol and diltiazem. You’re off telemetry now—your rhythm is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re planning to discharge you. You’re feeling better, infections are clearing, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue IV vancomycin twice daily for five more days—nurse visits will help. Then switch to oral vancomycin for two more weeks for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my myeloma meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start ixazomib as an outpatient. Follow-up with your oncologist next week. They’ll monitor the knee pain and consider an MRI if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—can I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are on your list—except the bowel softeners, hold those while on diarrhea treatment. Your diabetes and hepatitis B meds continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Call if you develop fever, worsening pain, or new diarrhea. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming before discharge—your IV vancomycin schedule is clear, and the home health nurse will contact you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got the times written down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And your oncology appointment is set for Friday. They’ll guide the next steps for your myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your discharge paperwork and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your pain is controlled with the lidocaine patch and oxycodone as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. Still aches, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep using the patch. If pain worsens, call your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home with home health services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take it easy, and we’ll see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick follow-up—your discharge summary is ready, and your medications are all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll review them at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us with any questions. You’re doing well—keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're here because your kidney function has worsened quickly. Your creatinine was 1.1 last time, but now it's 5.0. Do you have any symptoms like fatigue or swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No swelling, and I feel okay. I’ve been eating well. I did have some rib pain, but I’m only taking Tylenol and oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, no vomiting or diarrhea. Your urine output seems normal too. Given your multiple myeloma, this kidney issue is likely due to 'cast nephropathy'—a buildup of proteins from the cancer affecting your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because of the myeloma? I’ve had rising IgA and lambda chains lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your free lambda was 942 last week—very high. That’s likely overwhelming your kidneys. We’ll start treatment right away to reduce the protein load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start chemotherapy—CyBorD: cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone. We’ll also give you plasmapheresis to filter the harmful proteins from your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Plasmapheresis? How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a special line in your neck to remove your blood, filter out the abnormal proteins, and return the cleaned blood. It’s like dialysis but targets the myeloma proteins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And the chemo—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, CyBorD. You’ve had it before. We’re restarting it because your myeloma is progressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a kidney ultrasound this morning. Good news—it shows no blockage or stones. Both kidneys are normal in size and appearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s physically wrong with them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No obstruction. The damage is internal, from the protein buildup. That’s why chemo and plasmapheresis are key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll place the pheresis line in your right neck vein. It’ll be used for plasmapheresis over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local numbing and a little sedation. You’ll feel pressure but not sharp pain. The team will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was placed successfully. You’ll start plasmapheresis now. We’ll do three sessions over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I feel during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people feel fine. Some get lightheaded or chilled. We’ll give fluids and monitor your blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first plasmapheresis went well. We removed a lot of abnormal protein. Your creatinine is still high at 4.8, but we expect gradual improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for neuropathy, especially since you already have some. Bortezomib can worsen it. Let us know if your feet feel more numb or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—up to 170s. We’re increasing your carvedilol and diltiazem. We may add another medication if it doesn’t settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been stressed. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stress can play a role, but with myeloma and kidney issues, BP control is important. We’ll get it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Second plasmapheresis done. Your creatinine is down to 3.9. That’s a good sign your kidneys are starting to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Any update on my blood sugar? I’m on more steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sugars are higher. We’ve increased your Lantus to 46 units at night. You’ll need close monitoring after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re giving your second dose of bortezomib through the central line. How are you feeling overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but okay. My mouth feels dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you hydrated. Also, you’re still on vancomycin for C. diff. You’ve completed the intensive phase and are now on a taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll keep taking it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily at first, then every other day, then every third day. It’s to prevent another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your third plasmapheresis is scheduled. Also, your left leg has some swelling. We did an ultrasound to check for a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to rule it out. The ultrasound showed no DVT—good news. The swelling may be from inactivity or mild fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Plasmapheresis complete. Your creatinine is now 3.1. Kidney function is steadily improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big drop!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your free lambda is coming down too. The treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is better—150s now. We added doxazosin last night, and it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dizziness when standing up. Take it at bedtime, and rise slowly. It’s to help relax your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show creatinine down to 2.6. Nephrology agrees you don’t need dialysis. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow, if all goes well. We’ll remove the pheresis line in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on the same chemo regimen, with vancomycin taper, insulin at 46 units, and the new doxazosin for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin—what if my sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your morning blood sugar. If it’s below 100, cut the Lantus dose in half—down to 23 units—until you see endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We removed the line—no issues. Your vitals are stable, and labs confirm continued improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m ready to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll follow up with oncology, nephrology, and endocrinology. Keep taking all meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your team or go to the ER if you have trouble urinating, severe fatigue, shortness of breath, or very low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Keep up the good work, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your physical exam is stable—clear lungs, normal heart, no swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your wife pick you up. Make sure she reviews the discharge instructions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s on her way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Any questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Don’t forget your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got them. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final sign-out complete. You’re officially discharged. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re going home feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chart note completed. Discharge confirmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: All set. Heading home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I see you came in with abdominal pain and bloating. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. For the past three days, my belly has been really distended and painful. I haven’t had a bowel movement in three days, but I am passing gas. I also feel short of breath, especially when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you stopped your laxatives recently because you were having frequent bowel movements in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I thought I didn’t need them anymore, but now I regret it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. We’ve reviewed your labs and imaging. Your creatinine is improving—down to 2.1 from over 5—so your kidneys are recovering from the last admission. The abdominal X-ray shows moderate fecal load, but no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it just constipation causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a big part of it. You passed a large bowel movement last night, and you say your pain improved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it got much better after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. But because your symptoms didn’t fully resolve and you couldn’t tolerate food well, we ordered a CT scan. It showed inflammation in the duodenum—your first part of the small intestine. We’re calling it duodenitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Duodenitis? What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be from infection, medications, or even your multiple myeloma. One possibility is that your recent Velcade treatment may have contributed. We’ll need more tests to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an MRI today to get a better look. It confirms duodenitis with significant inflammation. There’s also a mass near your bladder—likely extramedullary hematopoiesis, which can happen with myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not a typical cancer, but it’s abnormal blood cell production outside the bone marrow. We’ll monitor it closely. The bigger concern right now is your belly pain and distention worsening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started hurting again this morning, and I feel very full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about a partial bowel obstruction. Your blood sugar also dropped to 36 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt shaky and confused. They gave me orange gel and an IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was D50. We’re switching you to a continuous dextrose IV to prevent more lows. Given your abdominal changes, we’re moving you to the ICU for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a nasogastric tube to decompress your stomach. It’s draining a lot of fluid—about 4 liters in the first 24 hours. This should help relieve the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels a little better already. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The imaging doesn’t show a blockage or perforation. This looks like pseudo-obstruction from inflammation. We’ll keep the NG tube in for a few days and see if your gut starts working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG output has decreased to less than 200 mL in the last 12 hours—that’s a good sign. We’re going to try giving you small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’m thirsty. What about the low blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your C-peptide and insulin levels. Your insulin was high but C-peptide low—this suggests you may have been getting too much insulin at home, especially with poor food intake here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 46 units at night because of steroids. Should I go back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. The endocrine team recommends holding long-acting insulin for now and using only sliding scale. We’ll restart it slowly once you’re eating regularly and off steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We removed the NG tube this morning. You tolerated a soft diet yesterday without vomiting or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad that tube is out. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We still need to address your multiple myeloma. Your IgA levels are rising again, and your blood counts are dropping—this suggests relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the cancer is active again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re starting you on high-dose dexamethasone for four days, followed by a Cytoxan infusion. This will help control the myeloma and may improve your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed the steroid course. Your blood pressure went up to 180s, but that’s expected with steroids. It’s coming down now that we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a bit jittery. My sugars were high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they reached 500. We adjusted your insulin and will taper it as the steroids wear off. Your liver enzymes are also mildly elevated—could be from medication or hepatitis B. We’ll check your viral load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HBV viral load came back—no detectable virus. That’s good. We’ll keep you on lamivudine. We also did a colonoscopy to check for colon cancer, given your history with Strep bovis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No cancer found. You had some benign polyps removed. We also did an EGD—your duodenum shows inflammation, but no ulcer or mass. Biopsies are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.5—much better. Your kidney function continues to improve. We’re discharging you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the mass near my bladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent urine cytology—it showed atypical cells. You’ll need follow-up with urology to check it further. Could be related to the extramedullary hematopoiesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re moving your bowels regularly and eating well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the walker like they showed me. I feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We restarted your CPAP for sleep apnea. You tolerated it well. You’ll need a new machine—your old provider lost their license.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we gave you a dose of Cytoxan yesterday. Your oncologist, Dr. ___, will see you soon to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call his office. What about my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on 16 units of Lantus at bedtime and Humalog sliding scale. Check your sugars before meals and at bedtime. If over 250, use the high-dose scale; if lower, use your usual one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—carvedilol, diltiazem, doxazosin. Just get your pressure checked at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged. Keep all your follow-ups: oncology, urology, GI for biopsy results, and endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in. How are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Bowels are regular, no pain. I started the vancomycin taper as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep up with the laxatives and PPI for your stomach. Call if you have fever, vomiting, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EGD biopsies came back—no infection or malignancy, just chronic inflammation. Continue the pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any update on the bladder mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urology has scheduled you for a cystoscopy. We’ll get more answers soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are stable. No need for further action now. Keep monitoring them at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 7.5. No transfusion needed. Continue B12 and folate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you took the single dose of furosemide on the day we discussed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did. Felt a bit more urination that day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That was just to help with any fluid retention from the steroids. No need to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets are improving—up to 43,000. That’s a good sign your bone marrow is recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any more nosebleeds or bruising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Keep using the nasal saline to prevent dryness from CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last call. Make sure you schedule your repeat colonoscopy in one year, as recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already called. They said six months might be better given my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Just stay on top of it. Otherwise, you’re doing very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We infused your Cytoxan safely. Oncology will guide next steps. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I’ll see Dr. ___ next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your discharge labs show stable kidney function, improved blood counts, and no infection. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lucky to be here. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right track. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder—your wife is listed as your contact. Make sure she has all the discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s picking me up soon. She’s been amazing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your hepatitis B remains inactive. Continue lamivudine as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll get the CPAP sorted with my PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set for a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urology appointment is confirmed for tomorrow at 1 PM. They’ll discuss the next steps for the perivesicular mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI follow-up is scheduled for next week to review the biopsy results in detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to ask about the duodenitis treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll likely continue the PPI and monitor for symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think we’ve covered everything. Thank you for your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in last night after your wife noticed you were confused and weak. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember eating dinner… then things got fuzzy. My wife said I was trembling and couldn’t answer her. I felt weak, like I couldn’t stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were febrile and tachycardic when you arrived. We did a CT scan and found pneumonia in your left lower lung, likely from aspirating food while eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspirating? I did cough a little at dinner. But pneumonia? I’ve been feeling tired the past few days, had a low-grade fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. The scan showed consolidation in the lower lobe, consistent with aspiration pneumonia. You’re on antibiotics—vancomycin, cefepime, and levofloxacin—to cover all possible causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on a lot of meds already. I was worried I didn’t have my heart pills—diltiazem and carvedilol—since the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held them initially because your blood pressure was high and you were septic. But now that you’re stable, we’ve restarted your usual doses. Your heart rate is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My multiple myeloma has been tough lately. I’m on daratumumab now. Is that safe to continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we plan to give you your next cycle once you’re stable. Your oncology team is involved. But first, we need to treat this infection and make sure you’re strong enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My last admission was for abdominal issues—distention, constipation. I’m glad that’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed that. You had a perivesicular mass thought to be extramedullary hematopoiesis. The CT today shows it’s slightly larger—5.6 cm—and still likely related to your myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s growing? Could that be causing problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It’s pressing on your bladder, which might contribute to your urinary incontinence. We’ll follow it closely with your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some incontinence since my prostate surgery. But this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. One episode occurred after sedating meds—trazodone and oxycodone. We’ve adjusted your pain regimen to reduce that risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I don’t want to be over-sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria grew. That’s reassuring. But your B-glucan level is elevated—348 pg/mL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Does it mean I have a fungal infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It can be elevated due to bacterial infections or recent antibiotics. The infectious disease team thinks it’s likely not fungal. But we’ll follow up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. And my pneumonia—how’s it doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re improving. You’re off supplemental oxygen and your fever is gone. We’ll continue antibiotics for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are trending well. Creatinine is 1.2—stable for you. Glucose is 157, better than admission. We’re watching your diabetes closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had issues with hypoglycemia before, especially when steroids were involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your last admission. You’re not on steroids now, so we’ve kept your insulin regimen stable. We’ll continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling stronger. Can I start walking a bit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Physical therapy will come by to help you ambulate safely. Staying mobile helps with recovery and prevents complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you IVIG yesterday—30 grams. No reactions, which is great. It helps support your immune system, especially with myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel anything unusual. That’s good. When will I get my next daratumumab dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling it for day 4 of your admission—so likely tomorrow. You’ll get it through your Port-A-Cath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got your daratumumab dose this morning. No infusion reactions. You’re doing well—your oxygen levels are normal, and you’re eating regular meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much clearer mentally. That confusion scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was likely due to the infection and fever. As your body fought it, your brain function dipped. Now that you’re treating the cause, you’re back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some pain in my left groin last night. It’s better now, but I felt a bulge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a CT. It shows a soft tissue mass in the left inguinal region—about 2.3 x 3.2 cm. It’s unchanged from prior scans and may be a hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A hematoma? From what? I haven’t injured myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to prior surgery or minor trauma you don’t recall. Since it’s stable and your pain resolved, we’ll follow up outpatient with an ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You received IVIG again yesterday—no issues. Your WBC is improving—up to 4.5. That’s a good sign your bone marrow is recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been pancytopenic for a while. Any sign of infection risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neutrophil count is still low, but stable. We’re being cautious with infection control. No fever, no new symptoms—that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my CPAP at night. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Sleep apnea can worsen oxygen levels, especially with lung infection. We’ll recommend a follow-up sleep study after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CT chest shows the pneumonia is improving—most of the opacities have resolved. We’ll switch you to oral levofloxacin to finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m close to going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well, discharge in 1–2 days. We’ll make sure your pain, diabetes, and heart meds are all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got your daratumumab dose today—cycle 4. No issues. Your labs are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the masses—pelvic and groin? Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pelvic mass is likely extramedullary hematopoiesis—blood cells forming outside the bone marrow. It’s slightly larger but stable. The groin mass is likely a benign hematoma. Both need outpatient imaging follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my B-glucan? Should I get that rechecked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your infectious disease team recommends repeating it in a few weeks, along with a non-contrast chest CT to monitor for any fungal concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is set for tomorrow. You’ll go home on levofloxacin for 7 more days, and all your usual medications, including insulin and heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oncology in one week for labs and daratumumab cycle 5. Urology for the pelvic mass. And primary care for the groin ultrasound and B-glucan repeat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep those. I’ve been through a lot, but I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done very well. Your mental status is clear, you’re walking independently, and your infection is resolved. We’re confident you’ll continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your discharge labs are good. Hemoglobin 8.0, platelets 25,000—low but stable. Creatinine 1.2. We’ll monitor those at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my counts are always low. As long as I’m not bleeding or feeling weak, I’m okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep an eye on it. One new med—gabapentin 400 mg twice daily for your neuropathy. Helps with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had burning in my feet. Hope that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed the CT from yesterday. The pelvic mass is still suggestive of extramedullary hematopoiesis. The groin mass remains stable. Outpatient ultrasound is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll get it done. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, shortness of breath, worsening pain, or confusion—call your doctor. Otherwise, rest, stay hydrated, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’ve recovered well from pneumonia, got your chemo, and are back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Continue levofloxacin, all your regular meds, and follow up as scheduled. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you were feeling confused and had a fall. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling really weak and foggy for about three days. After my groin biopsy, I just felt wiped out. I didn’t have a fever, but I felt hot this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also had a productive cough recently, correct? And you missed your daratumumab appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a cough a few days ago, but it’s gone now. And yes, I missed my clinic visit—twice. I just couldn’t make it. I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve run some tests. Your calcium level is high—10.7—which can cause confusion and weakness. We’re giving you IV fluids and a medication called pamidronate to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that why I’ve been so out of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High calcium from your multiple myeloma can affect your brain. As your levels improve, your mental clarity should return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my kidneys? My creatinine is up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine is 1.7, but your baseline is 1.1. This acute kidney injury is likely due to dehydration and high calcium. IV fluids are helping, and we expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood sugar? I’m on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 285, so we’re managing it with your usual insulin—Glargine at night and Humalog with meals, plus sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. What about that blood culture result I heard about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One blood culture showed coagulase-negative staph. But since you’re not febrile and only one bottle grew it, it’s likely a skin contaminant. We started vancomycin just in case, but may stop it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. We’ll repeat blood cultures tomorrow to confirm it’s not a real infection. If they’re negative, we’ll discontinue the IV vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart? I’m on diltiazem and carvedilol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing both for your atrial tachycardia. Your heart rate is stable now, around 114, and regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my eye? It’s been red and itchy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted mild left eye injection. It’s improved. We’ll start artificial tears and a short course of Tobradex drops for possible episcleritis. Follow up with ophthalmology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my bowel movements? I’ve been constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT showed a large fecal load. We’ve restarted your polyethylene glycol and bisacodyl. Staying regular is important, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That confirms the staph was likely a contaminant. We’re stopping vancomycin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, so no more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. But you’ll continue your oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention daily for two weeks, then discuss frequency with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. How’s my calcium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s coming down—now 9.3. Your mental status is much clearer, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel more like myself. And my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is down to 1.4. With continued hydration, we expect it to reach your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test was negative for C. diff. That’s good—we can keep focusing on constipation management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my myeloma? I missed my daratumumab dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last dose was delayed. Your oncologist will reschedule cycle 8 soon. Your IgA is still high at 1630, so continuing treatment is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure not to miss it next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help coordinate that. In the meantime, your biopsy site is healing well, and the mass looks stable on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Calcium is 9.1, creatinine is 1.2, and hemoglobin is stable. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds, especially insulin, lamivudine for Hep B, and stool softeners. Take oral vancomycin daily for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use the Tobradex three times a day for seven days, and artificial tears four times a day. Call ophthalmology for a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—confusion, fever, chills, or trouble breathing. Those could mean your calcium is up or an infection. Come back right away if they happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my wife has my contact info if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll also send a note to your primary doctor and oncologist. Make sure to keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final blood cultures are negative. You’re doing well—clear mentally, stable vitals, and labs improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you with services to help at home. Continue all medications as discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. The high calcium was the main issue, and we’ve corrected that. Keep up with hydration and bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
